title: Booking system class diagram
idea: A class diagram fixes who knows whom: `BookingService` sits in the middle and talks only to interfaces, so storage, conflict rules and notifications can change behind them.
points: Draw entities first, then the service, then each dependency as an interface.
Arrows point toward what a class depends on; the service's arrows end at interfaces.
Each interface takes the narrowest signature its single caller needs, nothing more.
Interviewers read the diagram first; mark multiplicity where it matters, like `0..*` listeners.

hero.title: Service at the centre, interfaces around it

steps.caption: Start from the entities found in requirements: `Booking` points to `Room` by id only.
`BookingService` owns the use cases. It holds the rules but no storage or delivery code.
Storage hides behind two repository interfaces, one per entity the service loads.
The overlap rule is an interface too, because buffer times or priority rules may replace it.
Side effects go out through `BookingListener`. The service holds zero or more of them.
Concrete listeners implement the interface. Adding Slack alerts adds a class; the service is untouched.

code.title: Diagram as code
code.caption: Mermaid text for the same diagram. It lives in the repository and changes in the same pull request as the code.

walk.text: The service lists only its public use-case methods. Private helpers stay off the diagram.
Repositories are marked `<<interface>>`. Their methods are what the service needs, not generic CRUD.
`ConflictPolicy` and `BookingListener` are the two extension points of the design.
Solid arrows are associations: the service stores each as a field. `0..*` allows zero listeners.
Dotted arrows with a hollow head mean 'implements'. Both concrete listeners are interchangeable.
Composition: a room cannot exist without its building. A booking only refers to room and employee.

code.title: Interfaces in Java
code.caption: The diagram's interfaces, compiled. Each is usable alone with a lambda or a small in-memory class.

walk.text: Lookups take ids and return `Optional` or `List`, never null; implementations return copies, not live views.
`ConflictPolicy` has one method, so a lambda can implement it in a test or a demo.
A default `onCancelled` lets a listener that only cares about new bookings stay one method.
The in-memory repository uses a `TreeMap` and returns `List.copyOf`, so callers cannot edit its state.
Main wires a repository, a policy and a listener without any `BookingService` yet.
Overlap is caught, a back-to-back slot is not, and a missing id returns an empty `Optional`.

pitfalls: Drawing every getter and setter buries the dependencies; show only methods other classes call.
Pointing arrows from interface to service reverses the dependency and hides who can be swapped.
A repository interface with twenty generic methods leaks storage details into the service.

quiz.q: After the demo, what does this print?
quiz.code:
Booking b4 = new Booking("B4", "R2", "e3", 9.5, 10.5);
System.out.println(overlap.conflicts(b4, repo.forRoom("R1")));
quiz.why: The lambda compares times only. It trusts the caller to pass bookings of the same room, so B1 in R1 counts as a clash.

takeaway: Put the service in the middle and every changeable part behind an interface.

starters: Should ConflictPolicy check that bookings are in the same room?
